definition: Hereditary means passed down genetically from parent to offspring.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hereditary. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hereditary should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The breeder traced the hereditary coat pattern through six generations of her herd.
Familial says only that a trait runs in a family, which could be diet or habit as easily as descent, while hereditary says it travels in the genes.
Genetic is the most precise of the three, since every hereditary trait is genetic, but a genetic change arising new in one individual is not hereditary until it is passed on.

Inherited is the everyday word for anything received from those who came before, from a grandmother's ring to a gene for eye colour. Hereditary is the formal adjective for what descent itself transmits, and in medicine it points specifically to transmission through the parents' genes.

Ancestral ties something to one's forebears -- ancestral land, an ancestral custom -- without saying how it travelled down. Hereditary names the mechanism: passed from parent to offspring, in medicine through the genes. A recipe can be ancestral; a blood type is hereditary.

A vet compiles records on 240 collies living in one valley.

A particular eye defect appears in 61 of them, and every single affected dog descends from one imported sire; not one dog outside his line shows it, though all 240 share the same pastures, water, and feed.
Two litters raised in different counties turn up the same defect in the same proportion.
The vet concludes that the condition is hereditary.

The defect follows one sire's bloodline rather than the shared pasture, water, or feed, and reappears in pups raised elsewhere, which marks a trait travelling by descent, exactly what hereditary means.
technical in biology and law; neutral
Hereditary covers anything transmitted by descent, whether a gene, a title, or a monarchy.

In medicine it is the narrower cousin of congenital, taught in this unit: congenital means only that a condition was present at birth, while hereditary specifies that it arrived through the parents' genes.

In 1853 Queen Victoria's youngest son, Leopold, bled alarmingly from small scrapes, and the palace doctors could neither explain it nor stop it.
The disorder, haemophilia, was hereditary: it travelled through the family's genes, passed from mother to son in a pattern no physician of the day could yet read.
Victoria's daughters showed no symptoms themselves, yet several of their sons developed the same fragile blood.
Nothing about palace life caused it.
Royal cousins raised in different countries, on different diets, under different doctors, bled the same way.
The trait was not a habit of the household but a fact of descent, written into the line itself.
